translation:
<meta>This page continues the previous discussion regarding the vanity of worldly pursuits, specifically focusing on the fragility of wealth and the physical consequences of a life of pleasure, framing these misfortunes as spiritual "Crosses."</meta>

->### Chap. VII. On External Crosses.<-

—many goods, *Luke XII. v. 19.* <note>The text completes the biblical quote started on the previous page: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years..."</note> A ship has just perished at sea, which was carrying a good and large portion of his fortune; or a major bankruptcy occurs at the bank of Venice, or of Amsterdam: where are his riches? The rich man awakes from his sleep; and he finds nothing in his hands of the treasures he had dreamt of. On another side, it <note>The "Wisdom of the Cross" mentioned on the previous page.</note> places before our eyes a voluptuary <note>A person devoted to luxury and sensual pleasures.</note>, who has consumed his wealth and his health in fine dining and in other pleasures, which modesty forbids naming: Here he is, nailed to a bed, or to an armchair by the gout, which his debauches <note>Historical term for excessive indulgence in physical pleasures, which was commonly believed to cause ailments like gout.</note> have brought upon him: What has become of his pleasures? They have become for him a continual torment and a painful repentance: as many pleasures, so many torments; where one has sinned, there one is punished. But the man sensitive to the ills of the body remains almost always insensitive to the ills of the soul; until finally his time passes, and God's time comes after this life: it is then that one will pay dearly <note>Original: "payera la folle enchere." Literally "to pay the foolish overbid," an idiom meaning to suffer the heavy consequences of one's reckless choices.</note>, and one will read the chapter on Crosses after death.

V. If we were well persuaded that all our crosses are ordained, measured, and proportioned to the capacity

<sig>F 4</sig>

<vocab>Cross, Luke XII. v. 19, ship, fortune, bankruptcy, Venice, Amsterdam, voluptuary, fine dining, gout, debauches, repentance, punished, ills of the soul, paying dearly</vocab>

<summary>This page describes how worldly losses (like shipwrecks or bank failures) and physical ailments (like gout) act as "Crosses" designed to detach the soul from material and sensual idols. It warns that those who ignore their spiritual failings during life will be forced to confront them after death.</summary>
<keywords>Crosses, vanity of riches, bankruptcy, gluttony, gout, divine justice, repentance, Venice, Amsterdam</keywords>

Il capitello s'allontana molto da gli scritti di Vitruuio, perche egli è di maggiore altezza senza la cimasa, che non lo descriue Vitruuio con tutta la cimasa; et nondimeno per la comune opinione sono i più bei capitelli che siano in Ro-anco quei del portico; di maniera che io giudico, sì come da principio io dissi, non hauer trouato edificio fatto con maggiore osseruanza dell'ordine, quanto è questo: et s'io volessi scriuere tante belle osseruanze che vi sono, così dentro come di fuori, io parrei forse troppo prolisso; et perdì di questo marauiglioso edificio farò fine, seguitando dell'altre antichità.

translation:
### OF ANTIQUITIES

The four figures below here are members of the tabernacle beside this, as the letters A, B, C, D denote, which correspond approximately to the measurements of the heights stated here behind. But let it suffice for the Architect that all things, member by member, are diligently transported from the large ones and reduced to this form proportionally. And although perhaps to the students of <term>Vitruvius</term> this cornice will seem too high in proportion to the architrave and the frieze—and I for my part would not make it so high—nevertheless, seeing it in that place which has great distance and is not very high, it represents good proportion. The capital departs much from the writings of <term>Vitruvius</term>, because it is of greater height without the <term>cimasa</term> <gloss>crown molding/cymatium</gloss> than <term>Vitruvius</term> describes it with the entire <term>cimasa</term>. And nevertheless, by common opinion, they are the most beautiful capitals that exist in Rome, as are those of the portico. In such a way that I judge, just as I said from the beginning, that I have not found an edifice made with greater observance of the order than this is. And if I wanted to write of all the beautiful observances that are there, both inside and out, I would perhaps seem too prolix. And so, I will make an end of this marvelous building, continuing with other antiquities.

And may his heart be thin <note>meaning: sensitive/subtle</note> and soft and patient and deliberate. And his heart shall be bright and his face shall always shine. And all the work of action is the work of the body alone, and it is inferior to the level. And it is close to being, God forbid, like one who serves idols, and it is the action without intention (<term>kavanah</term> <gloss>focused intention/devotion</gloss>). And a man must strive for work that has both action and thought in it. And it is very close to being a completely pious and perfect person. And it is close for him to merit the Holy Spirit (<term>ruaḥ ha-kodesh</term> <gloss>divine inspiration</gloss>). And may his heart be bright and his face shine. And happy is the man who does for Him a perfect work. And may kindness and truth be upon his heart always. And may his heart be poor and crushed and praying. And he shall pray to the God of the heavens at all times. And he shall be careful and diligent in the work of his God. And may his heart be thin and soft and patient and deliberate. And may he be humble and persistent in Torah with every person always.

And may a man’s heart be clear of any evil thought in the world, and may it be clear and pure. And may his heart be attached to its Creator always. And he shall occupy himself with Torah day and night. <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the nature of the creature as an image of God. It concludes a sentence about the creature's existence within the Divine Being before expanding on the theology of the "Firstborn" as the mediator of creation.</meta>

### The Eighteenth Chapter.

...to preserve the quality of the image, to live within it, or to fall out of it; that is, to turn to the right or to the left.

The eternal, effortless <note>original: "wirckloſe." In this mystical context, it suggests a state of pure, undisturbed potentiality or "being" that acts without the labor or struggle associated with created things.</note>, self-sufficient, endless, true, uncreated, unborn Being or Good, has born from itself another Being out of its own essence, in order to reveal itself therein—and through it and with it—and to call all things into being, whether they be invisible or visible. This born Being, because it does not exist of itself and is not its own essence (unlike the unborn Being), is rightly called an Image, a Son, a Radiance, or a Reflection of the Divine Majesty; a Word, Arm, Will, or Law of **GOD**. 

For in this [Being], the eternal and unborn allows itself to be contemplated and seen face to face, as in an image and a mirror. Through and with this, **GOD** creates, works, and governs all things, as if by His arm, hand, or tool; through it, He judges all creatures, etc. Such an image of the unborn Highest Good is called the firstborn before all creatures, because **God** has born all things through him into image and likeness—especially the angel and the human, the rational, free-willed creature. 

Now it is decreed in eternity: whoever is not found to be conformed to this Firstborn, and does not remain one with him, shall be cast out from the Heavenly Paradise. This Firstborn is the Word of **GOD**, the Will and Law of **GOD**, the true Image of the eternal and invisible God. Within this, the creature should live; that is, it should keep and preserve the nature, kind, and quality of an image. Namely, it should not belong to itself, for it is not from itself; it should not seek nor love itself, but rather Him whose image it bears. It should not claim for itself anything that is called or named good; it should not take ownership of the will, but rather leave it free

translation: She saw Xiren with tears streaming down her face. Aunt Xue comforted and exhorted her for a while. Xiren was inherently honest and not the sort to be glib; she replied to every sentence Aunt Xue said, "I am but a servant. The Aunt takes the trouble to speak to me about these things. I would never dare to disobey the Mistress." Aunt Xue heard her words and thought what a gentle and obedient child she was, growing even more fond of her. Baochai also spoke of the great principles, and they all settled down in peace. A few days later, Jia Zheng returned home. Jia Zheng saw that Jia She and Jia Zhen had already returned. The brothers and nephews met and recounted the circumstances of their time apart. When the ladies of the inner household met them, they could not help but think of Baoyu, and all wept for a while. Jia Zheng stopped them, saying, "This is the way of the world. Now, we must manage the household affairs from the outside, and you must assist from the inside. We must not remain as lax as before. Each branch should manage its own affairs, and there is no need for a total centralization of our branch's business."

heretic, called Rokutsuponji, a reader of auguries, cunning in astrology and in the healing art. It happened, one day, that this heretic, being in company with Buddha, entered a forest, which was full of dead men’s skulls. Buddha, taking up one of the skulls and tapping it thus” (here the preacher tapped the reading-desk with his fan), “said, ‘What manner of man was this bone when alive?—and, now that he is dead, in what part of the world has he been born again?’ The heretic auguring from the sound which the skull, when struck, gave forth, began to tell its past history, and to prophesy the future. Then Buddha, tapping another skull, again asked the same questions. The heretic answered—

“‘Verily, as to this skull, whether it belonged to a man or a woman, whence its owner came or whither he has gone, I know not. What think you of it?’

“‘Ask me not,’ answered Buddha. But the heretic pressed him, and entreated him to answer; then Buddha said, ‘Verily this is the skull of one of my disciples, who forsook the lusts of the flesh.’

“Then the heretic wondered, and said—

“‘Of a truth, this is a thing the like of which no man has yet seen. Here am I, who know the manner of the life and of the death even of the ants that creep. Verily, I thought that no thing could escape my ken; yet here lies one of your disciples, than whom there lives no nobler thing, and I am at fault. From this day forth I will enter your sect, praying only that I may receive your teaching.’

“Thus did this learned heretic become a disciple of Buddha. If such an one as he was converted, how much the more should after-ages of ordinary men feel that it is through Buddha alone that they can hope to overcome the sinful lusts of the flesh! These lusts are the desires which agitate our hearts: if we are free from these desires, our hearts will be bright and pure; and there is nothing, save the teaching of Buddha, which can ensure us this freedom. Following the commands of Buddha, and delivered by him from our desires, we may pass our lives in peace and happiness.”

# GERMANIÆ PROSPERITAS.

One could make a trial of the same thing with worms originating from meat or cheese, and one will discover that this saltpeter is not denied to animals here. Therefore, nothing will be found in which that universal Salt of the World is not discovered. In some, however, the salt more quickly assumes the nature of saltpeter, while in others it has already been made saltpeter by Nature.

Let this be an example: the Essential or universal salt of vegetables, animals, and minerals is indeed naturally nitrous, but it does not catch flame until it has attracted life and flame from the air. However, one of the salts attracts that life more quickly and readily than another, just as it was formed by Nature. The more fleeting and urinous the salts are, the more quickly they change themselves into niter. The more biting and corrosive they are, the more difficultly and slowly they assume the nature of saltpeter. But because niter is a salt participating in both natures, namely urinous and corrosive, and is as it were composed of both, that is, of urinous and corrosive salt, the skilled man will easily assist nature with its aid and will make of them whatever he wills. Nor is there any salt in the nature of things that cannot be changed into niter with the help of art; especially those salts that are sublimated by fire and, raised by its force, ascend: such as those that are in the urine and excrements of all animals: indeed, animals, vegetables, and minerals themselves quite easily seize the nature of Niter. Let this be the first grade of salts. The second grade is of those salts that are somewhat more fixed, as the sons of art...

<summary>The author explains that all substances contain a universal salt that can be transformed into niter through interaction with the air. He classifies salts by their degree of volatility and corrosiveness, asserting that art can manipulate these natures.</summary>

Damis, who spent most of his time with Apollonius, was a native of the land of the Assyrians, and he first met him there in his own country; he recorded the association he had with the man from that time onward. ར ༣ ལ གཏན་མར་ལེན་པའི་རྒྱུ་ནོར་དངོས་པོའམ་ སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་མི་རྐྱེན་ དང་ རྩ་ཉེས་ཀྱིས་འཇིགས་བྱུང་ན་ གཏན་མའི་བདག་པོ་དེ་ལའང་རིན་ བབས་མི་ཐོབ་སྟེ་ གཏན་མ་དེ་ཉིད་བུ་ལོན་གང་ཞིག་ལ་བརྟེན་པ་ཡིན་རུང་ བུ་ལོན་དབང་བསྐྱོ་ཚབ་མི་ཐོབ། གཏན་མའི་བདག་པོ་དང་བུ་ལོན་ གྱིས་བདག་པོ་བཅས་གཉིས་ཀ་སྤྱོད་ལིན་གང་ཡང་བྱ་མི་ཆོག།

R 2-6 Regardless of whether it is state property, legal matters, living beings, or anything else, once it has been placed as collateral <term>gtan-mar</term> <gloss>collateral/pledge</gloss>, the one holding the collateral may maintain and care for it to improve its value. However, apart from the use of the collateral as security for the debt, one may not alter it, raise the tax burden associated with it, or impose any other penalties or collection actions that would harm the asset.

R 2-11 If the property or living being taken as collateral dies, is stolen, or is otherwise lost without the fault of the pledgee, the person who pledged the collateral must provide the full value of the lost item. All debts shall be managed according to the law.

R 3-1 If the property or living being taken as collateral perishes or suffers damage due to misfortune or natural causes, the owner of the collateral is not entitled to its value. Furthermore, regardless of which debt the collateral was intended to secure, the creditor is not entitled to compensation. Both the owner of the collateral and the creditor may not initiate any legal collection actions against each other.

<summary>This page establishes regulations for the handling of collateral, emphasizing that creditors cannot modify or over-tax pledged assets and clarifying liability in the event of the loss or death of collateral.</summary>

<header>COMMENTARIVS</header>
from the oration against *Vatinius*; Milo being accused by *P. Clodius* the aedile, as is clear both here below, and in the oration against *Vatinius*, and in Dio, book 39. Yet I would believe both were present in the same trial, since Cicero says, "These two, whom you see."

### O R A T I O.

I now omit Numerius, Serranus, and Aelius, the dregs of the Clodian sedition. Yet these, too, even now flutter about, as you see; and as long as you fear anything regarding yourselves, they will never fear for themselves. For why should I speak of the aedile himself? Who even set a day and accused Milo of violence. Yet he will never be brought by any injury to regret that he was of such virtue and such firmness of spirit toward the republic. But, to what will the young men who see these things turn their minds? That man, who attacked, razed, and burned public monuments, sacred temples, and the homes of his enemies; who was always surrounded by assassins, hemmed in by armed men, and protected by informers, of whom there is a redundancy today; who incited a foreign band of criminals, and bought slaves fit for slaughter, and emptied the entire prison into the forum during his tribunate—he flutters about as aedile, he accuses the man who in some measure repressed his exultant fury. This man, who protected himself in such a way that he defended his household gods in private matters, and the rights and auspices of the tribunate in the republic; he was not allowed by the authority of the senate to be accused moderately by the man by whom he himself is nefariously accused. Truly, this is that which you asked of me, most of all, in the accusation: what was our "party of the best men" <term>optimatium</term> <gloss>party of the best/aristocrats</gloss>. For so you spoke. You seek a glorious subject for the youth to learn, and one not difficult for me to teach. I will say a few words about this to the judges; and, as I think, my oration will not diverge from the utility of those who will listen, nor from our duty, nor from the very cause of P. Sestius.

<summary>This page covers Cicero's denunciation of Clodius and his cronies, contrasting their criminal behavior with the virtuous defense of the republic by Sestius and Milo.</summary>
